analysis.one_liner: Exempts all private economic agreements from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite America's core antitrust laws so they no longer apply to any voluntary agreement between people or groups of people. In practice, that would mean companies could fix prices, divide up markets, and merge into monopolies without breaking the Sherman Act, the Clayton Act, or FTC rules. Senator Rand Paul introduced it as a one-page bill, and no other senator signed on. It went to the Judiciary Committee and nothing further ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Large companies and dominant firms, which would gain near-total immunity from antitrust prosecution for price-fixing, market division, and monopolization as long as they frame it as voluntary agreement.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that the Sherman Act, Clayton Act, and FTC Act section 5 cannot be applied to any voluntary economic coordination, agreement, or contract between individuals or groups of individuals [S2][S3].
Senator Paul framed the bill as permitting voluntary economic activity, on the view that people should be free to associate and contract without government interference [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and workers, who would face higher prices, fewer choices, and weaker wages if antitrust enforcement against cartels and monopolies ended. Small businesses would lose legal protection against predatory conduct by larger rivals.

drawbacks.text: Antitrust laws exist to stop price-fixing cartels and monopolies; exempting all voluntary agreements would remove the main legal check on those practices, likely raising prices for everyday goods [S2].
The bill is one sentence long and contains no exceptions for conduct that harms competition, so it could not distinguish harmless cooperation from a price-fixing scheme [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is philosophical: maximum freedom to contract without government oversight. The cost is concrete: it would dismantle over a century of antitrust law, leaving price-fixing, market division, and monopolization effectively legal. The costs to consumers and competitive markets would almost certainly dwarf the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill in the Senate on March 16, 2016 [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced; the action record shows no further steps [S5].
The bill never advanced out of committee and received no vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and workers came out ahead, because the antitrust laws that protect them from price-fixing and monopolies stayed intact. Large firms did not get the immunity the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, since antitrust law stayed intact

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and it was referred to committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan lineup can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have given them immunity from antitrust prosecution for price-fixing, market division, and monopolization [S2]. Their gain would come directly out of consumers' wallets through higher prices. The bill died, so this never happened.
Without antitrust enforcement, small firms would lose their main legal shield against exclusionary and predatory conduct by much larger competitors [S2].
